Becker's Hospital Review: Hurricane Michael forced 5 Florida hospitals to shut down (Bay Medical Sacred Heart, Gulf Coast Regional, Select Specialty-Panama City, Emerald Coast Behavioral, plus one additional facility)

Florida Health Care Association (nursing homes, NOT hospitals - recorded for context): ~1,600 residents evacuated from 14 affected nursing homes - 10 evacuated before the storm, 4 after (Oct 12, 2018)

SC DHEC worked with 131 regulated health care facilities in the medical evacuation zones, including 17 hospitals, to evacuate more than 6,000 patients and caregivers to other facilities across the state

Seven hospitals in the SC evacuation zone were closed as of Saturday Sept 15 (named in state updates: Grand Strand Medical Center, Palmetto Behavioral Hospital, Tidelands Georgetown Memorial, Tidelands Rehab Hospital, Tidelands Waccamaw Community Hospital, Vibra Hospital of Charleston, plus one more); DHEC had moved more than 2,400 people from 114 healthcare facilities along the coast by Sept 17

SC Hospital Association: the Governor's initial mandatory medical evacuation order covered 19 hospitals in nine counties but was retracted 48 hours later; in the end the order affected only three hospitals in two counties (Grand Strand, Tidelands Georgetown, Tidelands Waccamaw in Horry/Georgetown)

More than 1,700 people had been evacuated from health care facilities along the South Carolina coast by Wednesday Sept 12 (a day and a half before landfall), and all 32 nursing homes/assisted-living facilities in SC's coastal region evacuated (facilities aggregate, includes non-hospitals)
An estimated 177 hospitals, nursing homes, and medical facilities were in the hurricane's path in South Carolina, and 40 hospitals in North Carolina (pre-storm exposure estimate)
Hurricane Andrew damaged or destroyed 59 health facilities/hospitals in Florida
The storm blew roofs off at least five hospitals in three Louisiana parishes (St. Mary, Terrebonne, Lafourche)

The EDs of the two hospitals serving one of the most severely affected panhandle counties operated through the storm, treating 996 patients in the 6 days before landfall vs 1,135 in the 6 days after (Oct 4-9, 1995); CDC surveillance reports no hospital evacuation
Around $1 million in damage to 'hospital' in Wilmington, NC (facility unnamed in source; likely New Hanover Regional Medical Center or Cape Fear Memorial - needs Star-News archive verification)
Floyd triggered evacuation orders for ~2.6 million coastal residents across five states (largest US peacetime evacuation to that date), the context for coastal hospital decisions in FL/GA/SC/NC

Louisiana Hospital Association 'Hurricane Katrina Evacuation Report' (compiled Aug 31-Sep 2, 2005): 1,749 patients occupied the 11 hospitals surrounded by floodwaters, which also housed more than 7,600 additional people (staff, families, refugees)

Urban Institute: none of the New Orleans hospitals evacuated in advance of Katrina; in some two dozen hospitals patients had to be evacuated afterward due to loss of power, water, and sewage service; a dozen or so hospitals not isolated by water evacuated by conventional transport while the 11 flood-bound hospitals required boats or helicopters

MCEER study (Arendt & Hess 2006): of the 15 acute-care hospitals in the immediate New Orleans area (5,649 licensed beds), all but three (Ochsner, East Jefferson, West Jefferson) evacuated in the days after Katrina; one week after the storm only 1,279 beds were available in the three open hospitals; 1,782 beds in seven open hospitals as of Jan 29, 2006, with eight hospitals still shuttered
New Orleans Times-Picayune estimate, Aug 31, 2005: 1,600 patients and 8,600 staff and family members awaited rescue at New Orleans hospitals (as cited in MCEER report)
House Energy & Commerce hearing (Jan 2006): the New Orleans region had ~5,063 acute-care beds pre-Katrina; post-Katrina capacity dropped to ~1,750 beds
Louisiana attorney general's post-Katrina investigation encompassed more than 240 deaths at five hospitals and 13 nursing homes (AP via Fox News, July 20, 2006)

More than 100 deaths occurred in New Orleans-area hospitals and nursing homes after Katrina when emergency backup power systems failed; about 200 related lawsuits were filed in Louisiana (ProPublica/NYT, 2010)
Final evacuation of Charity and University hospitals (Friday Sept 2, 2005) removed roughly 2,200 people, including 363 patients (CBS/AP, Sept 3, 2005)

Mississippi Gulf Coast: three acute-care hospitals were forced to close temporarily by Katrina; all 14 hospitals in the region, including specialty facilities, had reopened within roughly a year (The Hospitalist, 2006)
Only three hospitals in Katrina's direct path in the New Orleans area - Ochsner, East Jefferson General, and West Jefferson Medical Center - remained open during and after the storm

NYC OEM: approximately 7,100 patients from 43 health care facilities (hospitals, nursing homes, adult care) in Zone A and the Rockaways were evacuated before landfall - the first mandatory pre-storm healthcare facility evacuation in NYC history; OEM opened an interagency Healthcare Facility Evacuation Center (HEC) to coordinate. (Page returned 403 on direct fetch; figure captured via search excerpts of the OEM Biennial Report 2011 - verify against archived copy.)

North Shore-LIJ Health System (Health Affairs 2012 case study): 947 patients evacuated pre-landfall from its three flood-threatened hospitals (SIUH North, SIUH South, Southside) with no deaths or serious injuries.

HHS OIG report OEI-06-13-00260 (Sept 2014): of 174 Medicare-certified hospitals in the declared disaster areas of NY, NJ, and CT, 7 percent evacuated and most sheltered in place; 89 percent reported substantial response challenges (electrical/communication failures, fuel, transport).

NJ Hospital Association (via Kaiser Health News/HuffPost): only two NJ acute-care hospitals were evacuated (Hoboken University Medical Center - 131 patients - and Palisades Medical Center); ~100 NJ hospitals, nursing homes, and assisted-living facilities ran solely on generators; 11 nursing homes evacuated.
CBS News: five NYC hospitals were forced to evacuate for Sandy - New York Downtown Hospital, Manhattan VA Medical Center, Coney Island Hospital, Bellevue Hospital, and NYU Langone Medical Center.

NBC New York: Sandy's hospital closures removed more than 2,000 patient beds from the NYC system and wiped out approximately 3,500 nursing home beds, straining remaining hospitals (New York Hospital Queens at ~112% of maximum load).
Modern Healthcare (Oct 30, 2012): more than 1,000 patients were evacuated from New York metro area hospitals during/after Sandy without any reported loss of human life.

At least three Florida hospitals evacuated some patients after the storm passed amid damage and power loss (including 36 newborns from West Boca Hospital); 3.1 million households (~6 million people) lost power statewide
Every hospital in Miami-Dade, Broward and Monroe counties was operating on generator power after the storm (contemporaneous CBS4 Miami reporting)
Eight Florida hospitals evacuated because of their coastal locations ahead of the storm

Over 200 patients from Camden and Glynn County (GA) hospitals were relocated inland to Tift Regional (Tifton) and Cook Medical Center (Adel); Georgia Hospital Association coordinated coastal-to-inland transfers
Louisiana Department of Health: water-system failures (70+ public water systems down) forced 10 hospitals to evacuate some or all patients — 9 in Calcasieu Parish, 1 in Cameron Parish
Water outages forced hospital evacuations across Southwest Louisiana (LDH-reported, contemporaneous)

Gov. John Bel Edwards: no Tier 1 hospitals were evacuated pre-landfall because COVID-19 surge (2,450 hospitalized) left no receiving capacity — 'evacuating these large hospitals is just not an option'; hospitals sheltered in place under this constraint
Ahead of landfall, coastal Louisiana hospitals evacuated only their most critical patients (ICU-level partial evacuations) amid the COVID surge
Ochsner Health evacuated 165 patients on Monday Aug 30 from three hospitals in the Houma/Raceland bayou region; 160+ patients moved from Louisiana hospitals post-storm overall
FEMA: four Louisiana hospitals suffered damage from Ida and 39 medical facilities were running on generator power
Gov. Ron DeSantis: 10 Florida hospitals evacuated due to Idalia; 9 of 10 back at full operational status within ~24 hours post-storm

Texas/Houston area post-landfall: 5 hospitals closed and later reopened; 16 hospitals operating on generator power; hospitals crowded, admissions delayed and some ambulances waited ~3 hours amid the mass power outage (~2.7M customers)

Texas Hospital Association: sporadic reports of power, wind and water issues at some area hospitals, but no reports of significant damage and no reports of compromised patient care; no hospital evacuations reported
NRG Center opened as a 250-bed medical shelter for discharged hospital patients who could not go home due to power outages, to decompress Houston hospitals
Florida state response updates reported 3 nursing homes and 6 assisted living facilities evacuated; no hospital evacuations reported for Debby's Big Bend landfall

Texas Medical Center sustained roughly $2 billion in damage in the worst urban flood in U.S. history; basements of interconnected TMC hospitals and research buildings were completely submerged via the tunnel/garage network, and Memorial Hermann was closed to patient care for 38 days

Louisiana Office of Emergency Preparedness opened 5 of its 9 new regional state special-needs shelters for Lili, caring for 260 special-needs persons (vs. 2 shelters/27 persons for Isidore the week prior); ~900,000 coastal Louisianans were ordered or advised to evacuate. No named acute-care hospital evacuation was recovered from accessible sources for this storm
FEMA reported all eastern North Carolina hospitals were reopened by six days after landfall (implying temporary closures/reductions immediately post-storm)

Isabel disrupted Richmond's water treatment operations in 2003, producing the city's only boil-water event between then and January 2025 — a citywide utility failure that Richmond-area hospitals (VCU Health, HCA, Bon Secours) had to operate through (referenced retrospectively in 2025 water-crisis coverage)

A peer-reviewed regional study documented significant impacts on emergency department visit patterns and hospital admission rates across coastal southeastern Virginia hospitals from landfall through day 5, but no hospital evacuations were reported in accessible sources

Local officials reported all three Charlotte County hospitals (Charlotte Regional, Bon Secours-St. Joseph, Fawcett Memorial) sustained significant damage and were 'out of commission' immediately after landfall
HHS Secretary Tommy Thompson directed $1 million each in emergency aid to DeSoto Memorial Hospital (Arcadia) and Osceola Regional Medical Center (Kissimmee) after Charley

Health Management Associates reported storm disruption 'felt throughout the state and at all 14 HMA hospitals' in Florida during Charley and the subsequent approach of Ivan, with Charlotte Regional's operations suspended

Gov. Jeb Bush's first post-landfall briefing (morning of Sept 16, 2004) reported damage to Pensacola hospitals including Baptist, West Florida and Sacred Heart; retrospective coverage states all hospitals in Pensacola were damaged
